The dorsal column system (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus, then the medial lemniscus) carries fine touch, vibration and proprioception and crosses in the medulla; the spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature and crosses in the spinal cord; the spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum.

pain-referred.d: Nociception is the detection and signaling of tissue damage; pain is the unpleasant experience the brain produces from it. Referred pain is pain from an internal organ felt in skin or muscle, because both send axons into the same spinal segments and converge on shared second-order neurons.

general-special-senses.d: The general senses use sensory receptors spread through the body: somatosensation (touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain and position) and the visceral senses from internal organs. The special senses (smell, taste, vision, hearing and balance) have sensory receptors gathered in organs in the head. A sensory modality is one kind of sense; a submodality is a variety within it.

face-sensory-pathway.d: The route for touch, pain and temperature from the face: first-order neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, second-order neurons in trigeminal nuclei of the pons and medulla whose axons cross and rise to the thalamus, and third-order neurons to the face area of the postcentral gyrus.

umn-lmn.d: The two neurons of a voluntary motor command. An upper motor neuron has its cell body in the motor cortex or a brainstem nucleus and its axon inside the CNS; a lower motor neuron has its cell body in the ventral horn or a cranial nerve motor nucleus and sends its axon to skeletal muscle, the final common path.

corticospinal.d: The main tract for voluntary movement, running from the cerebral cortex through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, pons and pyramids of the medulla. About 85–90% of its axons cross at the pyramidal decussation and descend as the lateral corticospinal tract; the rest form the anterior corticospinal tract. The corticobulbar tract is its branch to the cranial nerve motor nuclei.
r: bulb, the old name for the brainstem

motor-modulation.t: how the basal nuclei and cerebellum shape movement
motor-modulation.d: The basal nuclei and cerebellum shape movement without sending commands to the spinal cord. The basal nuclei select movements through a direct (go) pathway and an indirect (stop) pathway acting on the thalamus; the cerebellum compares intended and actual movement and corrects it. Motor pathways outside the pyramidal tract were once called the extrapyramidal system.

motor-lesions.t: signs of upper versus lower motor neuron damage
motor-lesions.d: Upper motor neuron damage causes spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia (brisk tendon jerks), a Babinski sign (the big toe extends when the sole is stroked) and little wasting. Lower motor neuron damage causes flaccid paralysis with lost tendon jerks, marked atrophy and fasciculations. Paresis is partial weakness.

cerebellar-divisions.d: The cerebellum has a midline vermis, two lateral hemispheres and a small flocculonodular lobe underneath. Functionally, the vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) handles balance and eye movement, the spinocerebellum (vermis and nearby strip) posture and ongoing movement, and the cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) planning skilled movement. Inferior, middle and superior cerebellar peduncles join it to the medulla, pons and midbrain.

descending-brainstem-tracts.d: Motor tracts from brainstem upper motor neurons to the spinal cord: the vestibulospinal tract (balance and antigravity posture), the reticulospinal tracts (tone, posture and walking), the tectospinal tract (turning the head toward a sight or sound) and the rubrospinal tract from the red nucleus (arm flexors; small in humans).
r: entrance hall, named for a balance chamber deep in the skull

reflex.d: A rapid, involuntary, predictable response to a particular stimulus, produced by a fixed circuit of neurons. The same stimulus gives the same response each time, and a spinal reflex runs without the brain.

reflex-arc.d: The five-part circuit every reflex runs on, in order: sensory receptor, sensory neuron, integration center (one or more synapses in the spinal cord or brainstem), motor neuron and effector. Damage to any part can abolish the reflex.

somatic-visceral-reflex.d: A somatic reflex acts on skeletal muscle through one motor neuron from the CNS. A visceral (autonomic) reflex acts on smooth muscle, cardiac muscle or glands through a chain of two motor neurons that synapse in a ganglion outside the CNS, and it can excite or inhibit its target.

stretch-reflex.d: The contraction of a muscle in response to its own stretch. Stretch fires muscle spindles, whose sensory neurons synapse directly on the motor neurons of the same muscle (a monosynaptic reflex), while interneurons inhibit its antagonist. The patellar reflex (knee jerk) and every other deep tendon reflex are stretch reflexes.

tendon-reflex.d: A polysynaptic reflex started by Golgi tendon organs, which sit where muscle joins tendon and sense muscle tension. Rising tension inhibits the motor neurons of the same muscle through interneurons and excites its antagonist, damping the muscle's force.

withdrawal-reflex.d: The withdrawal (flexor) reflex is a polysynaptic reflex in which nociceptor signals excite the flexors and inhibit the extensors of the stimulated limb, pulling it away. In the crossed-extensor reflex, interneurons crossing the cord do the opposite in the other limb, which straightens and bears the weight.

neuro-exam-parts.d: The neurological exam is a structured set of bedside tests used to localize a problem in the nervous system. Its parts are the mental status exam (cerebrum), cranial nerve exam (brainstem and its nerves, including the corneal reflex), sensory exam (ascending pathways, including stereognosis and graphesthesia), motor exam (strength, tone, pronator drift and reflexes) and coordination and gait exam (cerebellum, including the Romberg test).

gcs.d: The Glasgow Coma Scale scores consciousness by adding the best eye-opening (1 to 4), verbal (1 to 5) and motor (1 to 6) responses, for a total from 3 to 15. A total of 8 or less is severe impairment, the usual working definition of coma.

stroke-signs.d: A stroke (cerebrovascular accident) is the sudden loss of function in part of the brain when its blood supply is interrupted: ischemic when an artery is blocked, hemorrhagic when one bursts. Its warning signs are taught as BE FAST (balance, eyes, face, arm, speech, time). A transient ischemic attack is a brief episode of the same signs with no dead brain tissue on a scan.

spinal-cord-injury.d: Damage to the spinal cord that cuts tracts at one level and destroys the gray matter there. A cervical injury causes tetraplegia (quadriplegia), weakness of all four limbs; a thoracic or lower injury causes paraplegia, weakness of the legs. A hemisection, damage to one half of the cord, causes same-side weakness and position-sense loss with opposite-side loss of pain and temperature.

gustation.d: The sense of taste. Taste buds hold gustatory receptor cells, epithelial cells with no axon that detect five taste qualities (salty, sour, sweet, umami and bitter) and pass the signal to sensory neurons in the facial, glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. Umami is the savory taste of glutamate.

olfaction.d: The sense of smell. An odorant dissolves in the mucus of the olfactory epithelium and binds an odorant receptor protein on an olfactory sensory neuron, whose axon passes through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb. Anosmia is the loss of smell.

eye-accessory.d: The parts around the eyeball that protect and move it: the eyelids, the conjunctiva lining the lids and covering the white of the eye, the lacrimal gland and the ducts that drain tears into the nose, and the six extraocular (extrinsic eye) muscles. The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve, the superior oblique by the trochlear nerve, and the other four and the levator palpebrae superioris by the oculomotor nerve.

eye-tunics.d: The three layers of the eyeball's wall: the fibrous tunic (the white sclera and the clear cornea), the vascular tunic (the choroid, the ciliary body and the iris around the pupil) and the neural tunic (the retina).

lens-humors.d: The lens is the clear, flexible disc behind the iris, held by zonule fibers. Aqueous humor, made by the ciliary processes, fills the space in front of it and drains into the scleral venous sinus; vitreous humor is the gel behind it. Glaucoma is damage to the optic nerve, most often linked to poor drainage of aqueous humor and raised pressure in the eye.

refraction-accommodation.d: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes between clear materials; the cornea does most of it and the lens the rest. Accommodation rounds the lens for near vision: the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonule fibers go slack and the lens bulges. Myopia focuses distant light in front of the retina, hyperopia behind it, and presbyopia is the age-related stiffening of the lens. Visual acuity is measured with a Snellen chart.

photoreceptors.d: The light-sensitive cells of the retina. Rods work in dim light, have one pigment and give no color; cones work in bright light, come in three kinds and give color and fine detail, and are packed into the fovea. Photoreceptors signal to bipolar cells, which signal to retinal ganglion cells, whose axons leave at the optic disc, the blind spot.

phototransduction.d: The conversion of light into a change in a photoreceptor's membrane potential. Light changes retinal from 11-cis to all-trans (photoisomerization), activating the pigment (rhodopsin in rods: opsin plus retinal). A G protein lowers cGMP, cation channels close, and the cell hyperpolarizes and releases less glutamate.

visual-pathway.d: The route from the retina to the cortex: optic nerve, optic chiasm (where fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross), optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and primary visual cortex. Each optic tract and hemisphere handles the opposite half of the visual field.

pupillary-reflex.d: The narrowing of both pupils when light enters either eye: optic nerve in, a midbrain relay, and parasympathetic fibers of both oculomotor nerves out to the iris sphincter. Miosis is a narrowed pupil; mydriasis is a widened one.

visual-streams.d: The two routes visual information takes beyond the primary visual cortex: the dorsal stream into the parietal lobe works out where things are and guides movement toward them, and the ventral stream into the temporal lobe recognizes what they are.

ear-regions.d: The external ear (auricle, ear canal and tympanic membrane) collects sound; the air-filled middle ear holds the auditory ossicles (malleus, incus and stapes) and opens into the throat through the auditory (eustachian) tube; the fluid-filled inner ear holds the cochlea, the vestibule and the semicircular canals.

cochlea.d: The snail-shaped hearing organ of the inner ear. Its three channels are the scala vestibuli (from the oval window), the cochlear duct and the scala tympani (to the round window). The spiral organ (organ of Corti), with its hair cells, sits on the basilar membrane under the tectorial membrane.

hair-cell-transduction.d: Hair cells are epithelial sensory receptor cells topped with a staircase of stereocilia joined by tip links. Bending toward the tallest stereocilium opens mechanically gated channels, K+ flows in and the cell releases more glutamate; bending away closes them and the cell releases less.

sound-transduction.d: Audition, the sense of hearing, turns sound into nerve signals. Frequency is heard as pitch and coded by the place of greatest vibration on the basilar membrane; amplitude is heard as loudness and coded by firing rate. Conductive hearing loss blocks sound in the external or middle ear; sensorineural loss damages the cochlea or cochlear nerve. The Weber and Rinne tuning fork tests tell them apart.

auditory-pathway.d: The route from the cochlea to the cortex: cochlear nerve, cochlear nuclei, superior olivary nuclei (where the two ears are first compared), inferior colliculus, medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, and primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. Each ear reaches both hemispheres.

vestibular-apparatus.d: The balance organs of the inner ear. In the vestibule, the utricle and saccule each have a macula whose hair cells are covered by an otolithic membrane topped with otoliths; they sense head tilt and straight-line movement. The three semicircular canals have a cupula that lagging endolymph bends when the head turns. Their signals drive equilibrium and the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), which turns the eyes opposite to a head turn.

pre-postganglionic.d: The two neurons in series in every autonomic motor pathway. The preganglionic neuron has its cell body in the brainstem or spinal cord and a thinly myelinated axon that ends in an autonomic ganglion; the postganglionic neuron has its cell body in that ganglion and an unmyelinated axon that releases transmitter from swellings (varicosities) onto cardiac muscle, smooth muscle or glands.

sympathetic-anatomy.d: The thoracolumbar division: preganglionic neurons in the lateral horn of T1–L2 send short axons through white rami communicantes to the sympathetic chain (chain or paravertebral ganglia) or through splanchnic nerves to the collateral (prevertebral) ganglia: celiac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric. Long postganglionic axons return to every spinal nerve through gray rami communicantes or run to the organs.

adrenal-medulla.d: The inner part of each adrenal gland. Its chromaffin cells are modified sympathetic postganglionic neurons without axons: stimulated directly by preganglionic fibers, they release epinephrine (about 80 percent) and norepinephrine into the blood.

epinephrine.d: The main hormone of the adrenal medulla (also called adrenaline). Released into the blood during sympathetic activation, it reaches cells throughout the body, including cells no sympathetic fiber touches, and keeps acting for a few minutes after the nerve signal stops.

parasympathetic-anatomy.d: The craniosacral division: preganglionic neurons in brainstem nuclei (leaving in cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X) and in sacral segments S2–S4 send long axons to terminal ganglia beside or inside the target organ (intramural ganglia), where short postganglionic axons reach the effector. It does not supply the skin, limbs or most blood vessels.

somatic-vs-autonomic.d: Somatic motor pathways use one heavily myelinated neuron that always excites skeletal muscle at a neuromuscular junction. Autonomic motor pathways use two neurons meeting in a ganglion, end in varicosities, can excite or inhibit, and act on cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands, which keep working if the nerves are cut.

cholinergic-adrenergic.d: Autonomic neurons named for their transmitter. Cholinergic neurons release acetylcholine: every preganglionic neuron, every parasympathetic postganglionic neuron, and the sympathetic postganglionic neurons to eccrine sweat glands. Adrenergic neurons release norepinephrine: most sympathetic postganglionic neurons.

norepinephrine.d: The transmitter (NE, also called noradrenaline) released by most sympathetic postganglionic neurons from their varicosities. It binds alpha and beta-1 receptor proteins strongly and beta-2 weakly, and its signal ends mainly by reuptake into the varicosity.

nicotinic-receptor.d: The acetylcholine receptor protein on every autonomic postganglionic neuron and on adrenal chromaffin cells. It is a ligand-gated ion channel, so it is fast and always excitatory; it differs in subunits from the nicotinic type at the neuromuscular junction.

muscarinic-receptor.d: The G protein–coupled acetylcholine receptor protein on every parasympathetic target and on eccrine sweat glands. Depending on subtype it inhibits (slowing the heart by opening potassium channels) or excites (contracting gut smooth muscle, stimulating glands). Atropine blocks it.
r: fly (the fly agaric mushroom, where muscarine was first found)

alpha-receptor.d: Adrenergic receptor proteins of the alpha family. Alpha-1 raises calcium in smooth muscle, so vessels in skin and gut constrict, the pupil's dilator muscle contracts and sphincters tighten. Alpha-2, often on the varicosity itself, lowers cyclic AMP and turns down norepinephrine release.

beta-receptor.d: Adrenergic receptor proteins of the beta family, which raise cyclic AMP. Beta-1 speeds the heart and strengthens its contraction. Beta-2, reached mainly by circulating epinephrine, relaxes smooth muscle (widening the small airways and dilating vessels in skeletal muscle) and makes the liver release glucose.

autonomic-drugs.t: drugs that act on autonomic receptors
autonomic-drugs.d: Drugs that bind autonomic receptor proteins. An agonist activates a receptor protein and an antagonist blocks it. Sympathomimetic drugs (albuterol, phenylephrine) mimic sympathetic effects; sympatholytic drugs (beta blockers) block them; parasympathomimetic drugs (pilocarpine) mimic acetylcholine; anticholinergic drugs (atropine) block it; nicotine activates the nicotinic receptor proteins of every ganglion.

dual-innervation.d: Supply of one organ by both autonomic divisions. The divisions usually have opposite effects (sympathetic speeds the heart, parasympathetic slows it) and sometimes cooperate (both stimulate the glands that make saliva). Most blood vessels, sweat glands, arrector pili muscles and the adrenal medulla lack it and get sympathetic fibers only.

autonomic-tone.d: The steady background firing of autonomic neurons at rest, which lets one division change an effector in both directions. Vagal tone holds the resting heart well below its own rate of about 100 beats a minute; sympathetic tone keeps most blood vessels partly constricted.

sympathetic-effects.d: The fight-or-flight pattern: faster, stronger heartbeat (through the cardiac accelerator nerves), constricted skin and gut vessels (through the vasomotor nerves) and dilated vessels in working skeletal muscle (through local chemicals and epinephrine), wider airways and pupils, glucose release from the liver, sweating, and slowed gut and bladder emptying. It can be widespread and is prolonged by adrenal epinephrine.

parasympathetic-effects.d: The rest-and-digest pattern: slower heart rate, narrowed pupils and near focusing, tears and watery saliva, more movement and secretion in the stomach and intestines, relaxed sphincters, emptying of the bladder and rectum, and narrowed airways. Effects are local and brief.

ans-central-control.d: The hierarchy that runs the ANS: the spinal cord holds preganglionic neurons and simple visceral reflexes; brainstem centers integrate reflexes for the heart, vessels, breathing and pupils; the hypothalamus integrates body temperature, water balance and energy stores; and the limbic system and cortex feed emotions and thoughts into the hypothalamus.

endocrine-system.d: All the hormone-secreting glands and cells of the body taken together: dedicated glands such as the pituitary, thyroid and adrenal glands, organs with a hormone-making part such as the pancreas, and scattered hormone-secreting cells in organs such as the stomach, heart and kidneys. Its parts are linked only by the blood.

hormone-classes.d: The four chemical classes of hormones: amine hormones (single changed amino acids), peptide hormones (short amino acid chains), protein hormones (long folded chains) and steroid hormones (built from cholesterol). Androgens are steroid hormones that drive male characteristics.

hormone-transport.d: Water-soluble hormones travel dissolved in the plasma; lipid-soluble hormones travel mostly bound to carrier proteins. Only free (unbound) hormone reaches target cells. A hormone's half-life is the time for half of it to be cleared from the blood.

water-soluble-mechanism.d: A water-soluble hormone binds a receptor protein in the plasma membrane. A G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, which makes cAMP; cAMP switches on protein kinase A, which phosphorylates target proteins in a phosphorylation cascade. Phosphodiesterase ends the signal by breaking cAMP down. Other pathways use IP3, DAG and calcium.

lipid-soluble-mechanism.d: A lipid-soluble hormone crosses the plasma membrane (steroids diffuse through it; the thyroid gland's hormones use transporter proteins) and binds an intracellular receptor protein. The hormone–receptor complex binds a hormone response element on DNA and changes transcription, so the cell makes new proteins over hours.

hormone-stimuli.d: The three triggers for hormone release: a humoral stimulus (a change in an ion or nutrient in the blood), a hormonal stimulus (another hormone) and a neural stimulus (a nerve signal).

hormone-interactions.d: The ways hormones combine at a target: permissive (one hormone is needed for another's full effect), synergistic (together they give more than the sum of each alone) and antagonistic (they push the same variable in opposite directions).

pituitary-gland.d: A pea-sized gland in the sella turcica, hung from the hypothalamus by a stalk, the infundibulum. The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) is glandular epithelium that makes six hormones; the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is nervous tissue that stores and releases two hormones made in the hypothalamus.

hypophyseal-portal.d: Blood vessels that link the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary: a first network of capillaries in the hypothalamus, portal veins down the infundibulum, and a second network among the anterior pituitary cells. A portal system is any arrangement of two capillary networks in a row joined by veins.

releasing-hormones.d: Hypothalamic hormones carried by the hypophyseal portal system that make the anterior pituitary release (releasing hormones: TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH) or hold back (inhibiting hormones: somatostatin, dopamine) its hormones.

tropic-hormone.d: A hormone whose target is another endocrine gland, making it grow and release its own hormones. TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH are tropic.

growth-hormone.d: A protein hormone of the anterior pituitary (GH, somatotropin). It drives growth mostly by making the liver and tissues release insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which makes epiphyseal plate chondrocytes divide and tissues build protein; directly, it breaks down stored fat and raises the glucose in the blood.

anterior-pituitary-hormones.d: Besides growth hormone, the anterior pituitary releases TSH (to the thyroid gland), ACTH (to the adrenal gland's outer layer), the gonadotropins FSH and LH (to the ovaries and testes), and prolactin (to the milk-producing glands of the breast).

osmoreceptor.d: Neurons in the front of the hypothalamus that sense plasma osmolarity. When it rises, they lose water, shrink and fire faster, driving ADH release and thirst.

thirst.d: The conscious urge to drink, produced by the thirst center in the hypothalamus when plasma osmolarity rises, blood volume falls or the mouth is dry.

adh.d: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin): a peptide made by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolarity rises or blood volume falls sharply. It makes kidney cells insert aquaporins so less urine is made, and at high levels it constricts small arteries.

oxytocin.d: A peptide made by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary. It strengthens contractions of the uterus in labor through positive feedback and makes milk flow out of the breast during nursing.

pituitary-disorders.d: Too much growth hormone causes gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults; too little in childhood causes pituitary dwarfism. Too little ADH effect causes diabetes insipidus (large volumes of dilute urine); too much causes SIADH (water retention and low plasma sodium).

axis-feedback.d: A hormonal axis is a chain of hypothalamus, anterior pituitary and target gland, each driving the next. In long-loop feedback the target gland's hormone inhibits both the hypothalamus and the pituitary; in short-loop feedback the pituitary hormone inhibits the hypothalamus.

thyroid-gland.d: A butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck, two lobes joined by an isthmus across the trachea. It is packed with follicles: spheres of follicular cells around thyroid colloid, whose main protein, thyroglobulin, holds the stored hormones. Parafollicular (C) cells lie between the follicles.

thyroid-hormones.d: Thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), lipid-soluble amine hormones made from tyrosine and iodine. T3 is the active form, mostly made from T4 in the tissues. They raise cells' oxygen use and heat production, increase beta-1 receptor proteins in the heart, and are needed for normal growth and brain development.

thyroid-regulation.d: TRH from the hypothalamus makes the anterior pituitary release TSH, which drives every step of thyroid hormone making and release and makes the gland grow. T4 and T3 inhibit TSH and TRH release by long-loop negative feedback.

thyroid-disorders.d: Hypothyroidism (too little thyroid hormone: cold, tired, slow) and hyperthyroidism (too much: hot, weight loss, fast heart). Graves disease, an immune protein that switches on TSH receptor proteins, is the commonest cause of hyperthyroidism. A goiter is an enlarged thyroid gland. Congenital (neonatal) hypothyroidism is found by newborn screening.

calcitonin.d: A peptide hormone released by the thyroid gland's parafollicular (C) cells when blood calcium rises. It inhibits osteoclasts and so lowers blood calcium, but in adults its effect is small.

parathyroid-glands.d: Usually four rice-sized glands on the back of the thyroid gland. Their chief cells sense blood calcium through a calcium-sensing receptor protein and release parathyroid hormone when it falls.

pth.d: Parathyroid hormone (PTH): the main hormone that raises blood calcium. It drives bone breakdown by acting on osteoblasts, which signal osteoclasts; makes the kidneys keep calcium and lose phosphate; and switches on calcitriol production. Too much is hyperparathyroidism; too little, hypoparathyroidism.

calcitriol.d: The active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), made when the liver and then the kidneys each add a hydroxyl group; PTH switches on the kidney step. It makes the intestine absorb calcium and phosphate. Too little in adults causes osteomalacia, soft poorly mineralized bone.

pancreatic-islets.d: Small clusters of endocrine cells scattered through the pancreas, about 1 to 2 percent of its mass. Beta cells make insulin, alpha cells make glucagon, delta cells make somatostatin and PP cells make pancreatic polypeptide. Also called the islets of Langerhans.

glucose-storage-terms.d: Glycogenesis is building glycogen from glucose; glycogenolysis is breaking glycogen down to glucose; gluconeogenesis is making new glucose from non-carbohydrates such as lactate, glycerol and amino acids, mainly in the liver.

insulin.d: The protein hormone of the pancreatic beta cells, released when blood glucose rises. It lowers blood glucose by moving GLUT4 carriers into muscle and fat cell membranes, driving glycogenesis and blocking glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; it also stores fat and moves potassium into cells.

glucagon.d: The peptide hormone of the pancreatic alpha cells, released when blood glucose falls. It acts mainly on the liver, switching on glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so blood glucose rises.

glucose-loop.d: The negative feedback loop that holds blood glucose, the concentration of glucose in plasma, at about 70 to 99 mg/dL fasting. High glucose makes beta cells release insulin, which lowers it; low glucose makes alpha cells release glucagon, which raises it.

diabetes-mellitus.d: A group of diseases with chronically high blood glucose (hyperglycemia) from too little insulin, too little response to it, or both. Type 1 is loss of beta cells to the immune system; type 2 is insulin resistance with beta cells that cannot keep up. Polyuria and polydipsia are its classic signs.

hypoglycemia.d: A blood glucose below 70 mg/dL. It triggers glucagon and epinephrine release (shakiness, sweating, a fast heart) and, as the brain runs short of glucose, confusion, seizures and loss of consciousness.

adrenal-cortex.d: The outer 80 to 90 percent of each adrenal gland, which makes steroid hormones from cholesterol in three zones: the zona glomerulosa (aldosterone), the zona fasciculata (cortisol) and the zona reticularis (adrenal androgens).

aldosterone.d: The main mineralocorticoid, a steroid from the zona glomerulosa. Released when plasma potassium rises or angiotensin II arrives, it makes the kidney reabsorb sodium, with water following, and secrete potassium.

raas.d: A chain of blood-borne steps: kidney cells release renin when pressure there falls; renin turns angiotensinogen from the liver into angiotensin I; angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), mostly in the lungs, makes angiotensin II, which releases aldosterone, constricts vessels and raises ADH and thirst.

cortisol.d: The main glucocorticoid, a steroid from the zona fasciculata released under control of CRH and ACTH, with negative feedback, a morning peak and a rise with stress. It raises blood glucose through gluconeogenesis, damps inflammation and keeps vessels responsive to sympathetic signals.

adrenal-androgens.d: Weak androgens, mainly DHEA, made by the zona reticularis under ACTH's drive. Tissues convert them into stronger androgens; they matter most in women, supporting pubic and underarm hair and sex drive.

stress-response.d: The body's hormonal and nervous response to a threat, described as the general adaptation syndrome: an alarm reaction driven by sympathetic nerves and epinephrine, a stage of resistance carried by cortisol and salt-keeping hormones, and a stage of exhaustion in which prolonged exposure to these hormones does harm.

adrenal-disorders.d: Addison disease is destruction of the adrenal cortex, with low cortisol and aldosterone, high ACTH and darker skin. Cushing syndrome is the effect of long-term glucocorticoid excess, usually from medication: central fat, thin skin, high blood glucose and raised blood pressure.

pineal-melatonin.d: The pineal gland is a small gland in the epithalamus whose pinealocytes make melatonin from serotonin. Melatonin is released in darkness and switched off by light, through a pathway from the retina via the suprachiasmatic nucleus; it signals night to the body's clocks.

thymus.d: A gland in the mediastinum, behind the upper sternum, where white blood cells of the immune system mature. It is largest in childhood and is gradually replaced by fat after puberty.

thymosin.d: A family of peptides released by the thymus's epithelial cells that help white blood cells mature in the thymus. How much they act as circulating hormones, rather than locally, is still unclear.

gonadal-hormones.d: The steroid sex hormones made by the gonads: testosterone from the testes, driven by LH, and estrogens and progesterone from the ovaries, driven by FSH and LH.

anp.d: Atrial natriuretic peptide, a hormone released by stretched muscle cells of the heart's upper chambers. It makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, lowers renin, aldosterone and ADH release, and dilates vessels, so blood volume and pressure fall.

epo.d: Erythropoietin, a hormone released by oxygen-sensing cells of the kidney when oxygen delivery falls. It acts on the red bone marrow to raise red blood cell production.

hypoxia-basic.d: Hypoxia is too little oxygen reaching the tissues; hypoxemia is too little oxygen in the arterial blood. Altitude and lung disease cause both; a large bleed can cause hypoxia without hypoxemia.

leptin.d: A hormone released by fat cells in proportion to fat stores. It acts on the hypothalamus to lower food intake and allow energy use, and it permits reproduction; most obesity involves leptin resistance, not a lack of leptin.

hormones-and-bone-growth.d: Growth in length at the epiphyseal plates is driven by growth hormone through IGF-1, needs thyroid hormones, speeds up with the sex hormones at puberty, and ends when estrogen closes the plates in both sexes.

performance-enhancing-drugs.d: Substances used to improve athletic performance, banned in sport (doping). Anabolic steroids, copies of testosterone, cause muscle hypertrophy but suppress the user's own reproductive axis; EPO thickens the blood; growth hormone misuse mimics acromegaly.

circadian-rhythm.d: A body rhythm with a cycle of about 24 hours that persists without time cues, such as melatonin, cortisol and body temperature. The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the master (biological) clock, reset daily by light.

blood-functions.d: What blood does: it transports gases, nutrients, wastes, hormones and heat; it regulates pH, body temperature and fluid balance; and it protects against blood loss (clotting) and infection (white blood cells and immune proteins).

plasma-proteins.d: The proteins dissolved in plasma, about 7% of it: albumin (most abundant, made by the liver; its osmotic pull holds water in the blood), globulins (transport proteins, plus immune gamma globulins made by white blood cells) and fibrinogen (the clotting protein that forms the threads of a clot).

formed-elements.d: The cells and cell fragments of blood: red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets, about 45% of blood volume. Platelets are fragments, not whole cells, which is why the group is called elements.

hematocrit.d: The percentage of a blood sample's volume made up of red blood cells, read from the packed red column of a spun sample (the packed cell volume): about 37–47% in women and 42–52% in men. The thin pale layer above the red column is the buffy coat of white blood cells and platelets.

hematopoiesis.d: The making of blood cells in red bone marrow. A hematopoietic stem cell (hemocytoblast) gives rise to myeloid stem cells, which make red blood cells, megakaryocytes (which shed platelets) and most white blood cells, and to lymphoid stem cells, which make the immune system's central white blood cells. Growth factors such as erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and colony-stimulating factors steer it.

serum.d: The clear fluid left when blood clots: plasma without fibrinogen and the other clotting proteins, which the clot used up.

blood-properties.d: Blood's physical characteristics: about 5 L in an adult (7–8% of body weight), always red (bright when full of oxygen, dark when not), pH 7.35–7.45, roughly four to five times as viscous as water, and, deep in the trunk, at the temperature of the organs around it. Whole blood is blood with nothing added or removed.

erythrocyte.d: A red blood cell: a flexible biconcave disc about 7.5 µm across with no nucleus or organelles, packed with hemoglobin. It makes ATP by glycolysis and lives about 120 days.

hemoglobin.d: The iron-containing protein that fills red blood cells and carries oxygen. Each molecule has four globin chains (two alpha and two beta in adults), and each chain holds a heme ring with an iron ion that binds one oxygen molecule.

erythropoiesis.d: The making of red blood cells in red bone marrow, from proerythroblasts through erythroblasts to reticulocytes, which lose their ribosomes in a day or two in the blood. Erythropoietin from the kidneys drives it in a negative feedback loop that senses the oxygen reaching the kidneys.

rbc-lifecycle.d: After about 120 days, macrophages in the spleen, liver and marrow engulf old red cells. Globin becomes amino acids, iron is recycled, and heme becomes green biliverdin and then yellow bilirubin, which travels on albumin to the liver, is conjugated and leaves in bile.

iron-handling.d: How the body moves and keeps iron: transferrin carries it in plasma to the marrow and other cells; ferritin stores it safely inside liver cells, macrophages and marrow; hemosiderin is a clumped, slowly released store. Most iron is recycled from old red cells.

jaundice.d: Yellowing of the skin, the whites of the eyes and mucous membranes when bilirubin builds up in the blood, from fast red cell breakdown, liver damage or blocked outflow of bile.

anemia.d: Too little hemoglobin to carry a normal load of oxygen, from blood loss (hemorrhagic anemia), too little production (iron-deficiency, pernicious and aplastic anemia, or too little erythropoietin) or early destruction of red cells (sickle cell disease, thalassemia).

sickle-cell.d: An inherited disease in which a single mutation in the beta globin gene makes hemoglobin S. When HbS gives up its oxygen it forms stiff fibers that bend red cells into rigid sickles, which block small vessels and are destroyed early. One copy of the gene causes sickle cell trait, usually without symptoms.

polycythemia.d: An abnormally high red cell count and hematocrit: primary (a marrow mutation, polycythemia vera, with low erythropoietin), secondary (raised erythropoietin, as at altitude or with lung disease) or relative (lost plasma). It thickens the blood and raises resistance to flow.

leukocyte.d: A white blood cell. Leukocytes keep their nucleus and organelles, number about 4,500–11,000 per µL of blood, and do most of their work in the tissues, squeezing out through capillary walls toward chemical signals.

granulocytes.d: Leukocytes with visible stained granules, all from the myeloblast: neutrophils (most numerous, many-lobed or polymorphonuclear nucleus, engulf bacteria), eosinophils (red-orange granules, attack parasitic worms) and basophils (dark granules holding histamine).

agranulocytes.d: Leukocytes without visible granules: lymphocytes (a large round nucleus almost filling the cell; mostly the cells of specific immunity, from the lymphoid branch) and monocytes (the largest, with a kidney-shaped nucleus; they leave the blood and become macrophages).

antigen-antibody-basic.d: An antigen is a molecule the immune system recognizes as a specific target, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a surface. An antibody is a Y-shaped plasma protein, released by cells descended from lymphocytes, that binds one antigen; with two or more binding sites it can link and clump cells.

leukocyte-counts.d: The white cell count and the differential count (each type's share). Leukocytosis is a count above about 11,000 per µL and leukopenia one below about 4,500. Leukemia is cancer of blood-forming cells in the marrow; lymphoma is cancer of lymphocytes growing mainly in lymph nodes.

platelet.d: A thrombocyte: a nucleus-free fragment of a megakaryocyte, 2–4 µm across, 150,000–450,000 per µL, living 7–10 days. Its granules and contractile proteins let it seal breaks in vessel walls and give clotting proteins a surface to work on.

hemostasis.d: The stopping of bleeding from a damaged vessel, in three overlapping steps: vascular spasm, the platelet plug and coagulation.

vascular-spasm.d: The contraction of smooth muscle in the wall of an injured vessel, caused by direct injury, chemicals such as thromboxane A2 and serotonin from platelets, and local pain reflexes. It slows flow for up to about half an hour.

platelet-plug.d: A soft plug of platelets over a break in a vessel wall. Platelets adhere to exposed collagen through von Willebrand factor, activate and release ADP and thromboxane A2, and aggregate as fibrinogen bridges them, a positive feedback that healthy lining confines.

coagulation.d: The conversion of blood into a gel as the enzyme thrombin cuts fibrinogen into fibrin threads. In the body, tissue factor with factor VIIa starts it and activated platelets host the burst of thrombin; in the lab model, the extrinsic (PT) and intrinsic (aPTT) pathways meet at factor X and the common pathway. Factors II, VII, IX and X need vitamin K.

clot-retraction-fibrinolysis.d: Clot retraction: platelets pull on fibrin with actin and myosin, squeezing out serum and drawing the vessel edges together. Fibrinolysis: tPA converts plasminogen, built into the clot, into plasmin, which cuts fibrin and dissolves the clot over days.

anticoagulants.d: Substances that slow or stop coagulation: the body's own antithrombin, protein C and the heparin-like molecules on the vessel lining, and drugs such as heparin (boosts antithrombin; works in minutes) and warfarin (blocks vitamin K recycling; works over days).

clotting-disorders.d: Too little clotting: thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count), hemophilia (an inherited lack of factor VIII or IX), von Willebrand disease. Too much: thrombosis, forming a thrombus in an unbroken vessel; an embolus is a mass carried in the blood, and the blockage it causes is an embolism. Thrombocytosis is a high platelet count.

abo.d: The blood group system set by sugars added to the H antigen on red cells: type A carries the A antigen, type B the B antigen, type AB both, type O neither. From infancy, plasma holds antibodies against whichever of A and B the red cells lack.

agglutination.d: The clumping of cells when antibodies, each with two or more binding sites, bind antigens on several cells and cross-link them. It is an immune process, not clotting, and is often followed by hemolysis.

rh-factor.d: The D antigen, a red cell membrane protein. Rh-positive red cells carry it; Rh-negative cells do not. Rh-negative people make anti-D only after exposure to Rh-positive cells, through transfusion or pregnancy.

transfusion-reaction.d: Harm caused by a transfusion; the most dangerous is the recipient's antibodies attacking ABO-incompatible donor red cells, causing agglutination, hemolysis, fever, dark urine, low blood pressure and kidney damage. O negative red cells are the universal donor, AB positive the universal recipient, and a crossmatch mixes the patient's plasma with the donor's cells to check before transfusion.

hdn.d: Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis): a mother's antibodies cross to the fetus and destroy its red cells. The severe form occurs when an Rh-negative mother, sensitized by an earlier Rh-positive baby, makes anti-D that attacks a later Rh-positive fetus; anti-D immune globulin prevents it.

heart-location.d: Your heart sits in the mediastinum, between the lungs, behind the sternum and on the diaphragm, with about two thirds of its mass left of the midline. Its apex is the pointed lower tip, at about the fifth intercostal space on the left; its base is the broad upper, back end where the large vessels attach.

pericardium.d: The covering around the heart: a tough outer fibrous pericardium of dense connective tissue, and an inner serous pericardium folded into a parietal layer and a visceral layer with a film of serous fluid (the pericardial cavity) between them. The fibrous layer plus the parietal layer form the pericardial sac.

heart-wall.d: The three layers of the heart wall: the epicardium on the outside (the same layer as the visceral pericardium), the thick myocardium of cardiac muscle in the middle, and the endocardium, an endothelial lining, on the inside.

cardiac-tamponade.d: Compression of the heart by blood or fluid collecting in the pericardial cavity. Because the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch quickly, pressure in the sac rises, the heart cannot fill between beats, and blood pressure falls.

chambers.d: The four spaces inside the heart: two upper atria that receive blood from veins and two lower ventricles that pump blood into arteries. Surface grooves (the coronary and interventricular sulci) mark their boundaries; auricles, pectinate muscles and trabeculae carneae are features of their walls.

great-vessels.d: The large vessels at the base of the heart: the superior and inferior venae cavae (into the right atrium), the pulmonary trunk (out of the right ventricle, splitting into the right and left pulmonary arteries), the pulmonary veins (into the left atrium) and the aorta (out of the left ventricle, rising as the ascending aorta and curving over as the aortic arch).

septa.d: The dividing walls of the heart: the interatrial septum between the atria, the thick interventricular septum between the ventricles, and the atrioventricular septum between the atria and ventricles.

av-valves.d: The valves between each atrium and its ventricle: the tricuspid valve on the right and the mitral (bicuspid) valve on the left. Chordae tendineae tie their cusps to papillary muscles, which keep the cusps from flipping into the atria when the ventricles contract.

semilunar-valves.d: The pulmonary and aortic valves, at the exits from the right and left ventricles. Each has three pocket-shaped cusps that fill with blood slipping back toward the ventricle and seal the opening; they have no cords or muscles.

fossa-ovalis.d: A shallow oval dip in the interatrial septum, seen from the right atrium. It marks where an opening between the atria sealed after birth.

wall-thickness.t: why the left ventricle wall is thicker
wall-thickness.d: The left ventricle wall is about three times thicker than the right because it pumps into the high-resistance vessels of the whole body and must generate about five times the pressure; heart muscle thickens when it works against a heavier load. On average, both ventricles pump the same volume per beat.

cardiac-skeleton.d: Four rings of dense connective tissue around the heart valves, joined into one sheet between the atria and the ventricles. It holds the valve openings in shape, anchors the heart muscle, and blocks electrical signals from crossing straight from atria to ventricles.

oxygenated-deoxygenated.d: Oxygenated (oxygen-rich) blood has just left the lungs, with its hemoglobin about 97 to 98 percent loaded with oxygen. Deoxygenated (oxygen-poor) blood has passed through the tissues and given up some oxygen, but at rest it is still about 75 percent loaded; both are red.

pulmonary-circuit.d: The loop that carries blood from the right ventricle through the pulmonary trunk and arteries to the pulmonary capillaries around the alveoli, where it picks up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide, and back through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. It works at low pressure.

systemic-circuit.d: The loop that carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle through the aorta and its branches to the capillaries of every tissue except the lung's air sacs, and back through veins and the venae cavae to the right atrium. It works at high pressure.

heart-pathway.t: path of blood through the heart
heart-pathway.d: The order blood takes: venae cavae, right atrium, tricuspid valve, right ventricle, pulmonary valve, pulmonary trunk and arteries, lungs, pulmonary veins, left atrium, mitral valve, left ventricle, aortic valve, aorta, body.

coronary-circulation.d: The heart muscle's own blood supply. The right and left coronary arteries leave the aorta just above the aortic valve and branch (left anterior descending, circumflex, marginal and posterior interventricular arteries); cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium.

mi-ischemia.d: Myocardial ischemia is blood flow to heart muscle too low for its oxygen demand; when it reverses it causes angina. A myocardial infarction (heart attack) is death of heart muscle from ischemia that lasts too long, usually a clot on a cracked fatty plaque.

vascular-anastomosis.d: A connection between two blood vessels. Where branches of two arteries join, blood can reach tissue by a second route, called collateral circulation.

systole-diastole.d: Systole is the contraction phase of a heart chamber and diastole is its relaxation and refilling phase. One cardiac cycle is one full heartbeat, from the start of one beat to the start of the next.

contractile-cardiomyocyte.d: A working muscle cell of the heart wall (a cardiomyocyte): short, branched and striated, with one or two central nuclei, many mitochondria, and intercalated discs whose gap junctions pass action potentials to its neighbors. It rests at about −90 mV and fires only when charge from a neighbor brings it to threshold.

l-type-calcium.d: Voltage-gated calcium channels in the sarcolemma and T tubules of cardiac muscle cells that open slowly on depolarization and stay open a long time. The calcium entering through them holds the plateau and triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

cardiac-ap.d: The action potential of a contractile ventricular cell, lasting about 250 to 300 ms: a fast sodium upstroke (phase 0), a small notch (phase 1), a plateau near 0 mV where calcium entry balances potassium exit (phase 2), repolarization by potassium exit (phase 3), and rest at about −90 mV (phase 4).

cicr.d: Calcium-induced calcium release: calcium entering a cardiac muscle cell through L-type channels opens calcium release channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases a much larger amount of calcium into the cytosol and starts contraction.

cardiac-refractory.t: the long refractory period of cardiac muscle
cardiac-refractory.d: In cardiac muscle the absolute refractory period lasts about 200 to 250 ms, because the sodium channels stay inactivated through the plateau. It lasts nearly as long as the contraction, so a new action potential cannot start until the cell is relaxing, and twitches cannot sum into tetanus.

autorhythmic-cell.d: A specialized cardiac muscle cell, also called a pacemaker cell, that depolarizes to threshold on its own with no outside stimulus. About 1 percent of heart cells are autorhythmic; they start and conduct each heartbeat's signal and contract only weakly.

pacemaker-potential.d: The slow, spontaneous depolarization of an autorhythmic cell between action potentials, also called the prepotential. It is driven by the funny current (Na⁺ in through HCN channels), falling K⁺ exit, and late T-type Ca²⁺ entry; its slope sets how often the cell fires.

sa-node.d: The sinoatrial node: a patch of autorhythmic cells in the upper back wall of the right atrium, near the superior vena cava. It reaches threshold first, so it is the heart's pacemaker; a rhythm it sets is called sinus rhythm. Bachmann's bundle and the internodal pathways carry its signal quickly across the atria.

av-node.d: The atrioventricular node: autorhythmic tissue in the lower interatrial septum, and the only normal electrical doorway from atria to ventricles. It conducts slowly, causing the AV nodal delay of about 0.1 second, during which the atria finish contracting.

ventricular-conduction.t: bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers
ventricular-conduction.d: The fast conducting path through the ventricles: the AV bundle (bundle of His) crosses the cardiac skeleton, splits into right and left bundle branches down the interventricular septum, and feeds the Purkinje fibers, a subendocardial conducting network. The moderator band carries part of the right branch to the right ventricle's front papillary muscle.

intrinsic-rates.d: The rate each part of the conduction system fires at when left on its own: SA node about 60 to 100 per minute (about 100 with no nerve input), AV node and AV bundle about 40 to 60, bundle branches and Purkinje fibers about 20 to 40. Any site other than the SA node that sets the rhythm is an ectopic pacemaker, or ectopic focus.

ecg.d: The electrocardiogram (ECG, also EKG): a graph over time of the summed voltage changes of the heart, recorded from electrodes on the skin. Each lead is one view, the voltage between a positive electrode and a reference; a standard 12-lead ECG uses 10 electrodes.

ecg-waves.d: The three deflections of a normal beat: the P wave (atrial depolarization), the QRS complex (ventricular depolarization, which hides atrial repolarization) and the T wave (ventricular repolarization).

ecg-intervals.d: Timed stretches of the ECG. The PR interval (start of P to start of QRS, 0.12 to 0.20 second) is mostly AV nodal delay; the ST segment (end of QRS to start of T) is the flat plateau when the ventricles are fully depolarized; the QT interval (start of QRS to end of T) spans the ventricular action potential.

arrhythmia.d: Any heart rhythm that is abnormal in rate, regularity, starting point or conduction; also called dysrhythmia. Examples are tachycardia (above 100 per minute at rest), bradycardia (below 60), heart block, atrial fibrillation and ventricular fibrillation, which is treated by defibrillation. An artificial pacemaker fires when the heart's own rate is too slow.

valve-rule.d: Heart valves are passive: a valve opens when pressure behind it (upstream) is higher than pressure in front of it, and closes when pressure in front becomes higher and blood starts to flow backward.

cycle-phases.d: The five phases of each heartbeat: ventricular filling, atrial contraction (atrial systole), isovolumetric contraction (both valves closed, pressure rising), ventricular ejection, and isovolumetric relaxation (both valves closed, pressure falling). Isovolumic is another name for isovolumetric.

heart-sounds.d: The sounds of each beat, heard as lub-dub: S1 (lub) from closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular systole, and S2 (dub) from closure of the semilunar valves at its end. A murmur is the sound of turbulent flow, usually through a narrowed (stenotic) or leaking (regurgitant) valve.

edv-esv.d: End-diastolic volume (EDV) is the volume in a ventricle at the end of diastole, just before it contracts (about 120 mL at rest). End-systolic volume (ESV) is the volume left at the end of systole, after ejection (about 50 mL at rest).

stroke-volume.d: The volume of blood one ventricle ejects in one beat: SV = EDV − ESV, about 70 mL at rest.

ejection-fraction.d: The share of the end-diastolic volume that a ventricle ejects in one beat: EF = SV ÷ EDV × 100. A normal left ventricular value is about 50 to 70 percent.

pv-loop.d: A graph of left ventricular pressure against left ventricular volume over one beat. It traces a counterclockwise loop whose corners are the four valve events and whose width is the stroke volume.

vessel-tunics.d: The three layers of a blood vessel wall: the tunica intima (endothelium on a basement membrane; in arteries, bounded by the internal elastic membrane), the tunica media (smooth muscle and elastic fibers; in arteries, bounded by the external elastic membrane) and the tunica externa, also called tunica adventitia (collagen). Large vessels carry their own small vessels and nerves, the vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum.

artery-types.d: Elastic arteries, the largest arteries near the heart, have many elastic fibers in the tunica media; they stretch during ejection and recoil in diastole. Muscular arteries, farther out, have a thick smooth muscle media and distribute blood to organs.

arteriole.d: The smallest artery, under about 0.1 mm across, with one to a few layers of smooth muscle. Arterioles are the main resistance vessels; their steady partial contraction, vascular tone, sets how much blood enters each capillary bed.

capillary-types.d: Continuous capillaries have an unbroken endothelium; fenestrated capillaries have pores through their cells; sinusoids have large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane. An arteriole feeds a capillary bed; metarterioles, thoroughfare channels and arteriovenous anastomoses can shunt blood past it; pericytes wrap the wall; vasomotion is rhythmic arteriolar contraction. Precapillary sphincters are described classically, but their role in humans is unsettled.

venule-vein.d: Venules drain capillaries and merge into veins, which carry blood toward the heart at low pressure. Veins have a thin tunica media, a thick tunica externa, a wide lumen and, in the limbs especially, venous valves; they are capacitance vessels that hold large volumes of blood.

venous-reservoir.d: The blood held in the systemic veins and venules, about 60 to 65 percent of the total at rest. Veins are highly compliant, so they store blood with little rise in pressure, and sympathetic venoconstriction can shift that stored blood toward the heart.

venous-return.d: The flow of blood back to the heart through the veins, driven by a small pressure gradient and helped by the skeletal muscle pump, the respiratory pump and venoconstriction, with venous valves preventing backflow.

varicose-veins.d: Swollen, lengthened, twisted superficial veins, usually in the legs, caused when venous valves become incompetent: blood falls back, pools and stretches the thin wall, which pulls the next valve open in turn.

aorta-parts.d: The named sections of the aorta: the ascending aorta rising from the left ventricle, the aortic arch curving over to the left, and the descending aorta, which is the thoracic aorta in the chest and, after it passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, the abdominal aorta.

head-neck-arteries.t: arteries of the head and neck
head-neck-arteries.d: The brachiocephalic trunk (right side only), the common carotid arteries, which split into external carotids for the face and scalp and internal carotids for the brain, and the vertebral arteries from the subclavians. The carotid sinus is the pressure-sensing bulge at the start of each internal carotid.

cerebral-arterial-circle.d: A ring of connected arteries under the brain, also called the circle of Willis: the anterior communicating artery, the anterior cerebral arteries, the internal carotids, the posterior communicating arteries and the posterior cerebral arteries from the basilar artery. It is an anastomosis that can reroute blood around a slowly narrowed artery.

limb-arteries.d: In the arm, one artery renamed at landmarks: subclavian, axillary, brachial, then the radial and ulnar arteries, which join in the palmar arches. In the leg: femoral (with its deep femoral branch), popliteal, then the anterior tibial, which becomes the dorsalis pedis, and the posterior tibial.

abdominal-arteries.t: arteries of the abdomen and pelvis
abdominal-arteries.d: The branches of the abdominal aorta: three single gut arteries (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric) and paired renal and gonadal arteries, ending in the common iliac arteries, which split into internal iliacs for the pelvis and external iliacs for the legs. The celiac trunk splits into the left gastric artery, the splenic artery and the common hepatic artery.

pulse-points.d: Places where an artery runs near the skin over firm tissue, so its pulse, the pressure wave from each heartbeat, can be felt: temporal, facial, carotid, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis.

venae-cavae-tributaries.d: The veins that drain into the superior and inferior venae cavae. Above the diaphragm, internal jugular and subclavian veins form the two brachiocephalic veins, which form the superior vena cava; the azygos vein joins it from the chest wall. Below, the common iliac veins form the inferior vena cava, which receives lumbar, gonadal, renal and hepatic veins.

limb-veins.d: Deep limb veins run beside the arteries and share their names (radial, ulnar, brachial, axillary; tibial, fibular, popliteal, femoral). Superficial veins run under the skin: the cephalic, basilic, median cubital and median antebrachial veins of the arm, and the great and small saphenous veins, which start from the dorsal venous arch of the foot.

dural-sinuses.d: The brain's veins drain into dural venous sinuses, channels between the layers of the dura mater with no smooth muscle and no valves. The superior sagittal and straight sinuses drain to the transverse sinuses, then the sigmoid sinuses, which leave the skull as the internal jugular veins. The cavernous sinuses lie beside the sphenoid bone.

hepatic-portal.d: The route that carries blood from the capillaries of the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas through the hepatic portal vein to a second capillary bed, the liver's sinusoids, before it leaves through the hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava.

blood-pressure.d: The pressure of blood in the large systemic arteries, which swings with each heartbeat between systolic pressure, the peak during ejection, and diastolic pressure, the lowest point just before the next ejection. It is written systolic over diastolic, for example 120/80 mm Hg.

pulse-pressure.d: Systolic pressure minus diastolic pressure: the size of each beat's pressure swing. It widens with a larger stroke volume or a stiffer aorta and narrows when stroke volume is small.

map.d: The average pressure in the arteries over a whole cardiac cycle, which drives blood through the organs. At rest it is estimated as diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure; the estimate runs low at fast heart rates.

vascular-flow.t: blood flow and the flow equation (vessels)
vascular-flow.d: The volume of blood passing a point per minute. In any vessel, organ or the whole circuit it follows F = ΔP / R: the pressure difference between the two ends divided by the resistance.

resistance-factors.d: Vascular resistance is set by vessel length, blood viscosity and, most strongly, vessel radius, because resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius⁴. Total peripheral resistance (TPR) is the resistance of the whole systemic circulation; most of it is in the arterioles.

pressure-profile.d: The way blood pressure changes along the systemic circulation: high and pulsing in the arteries, falling most steeply across the arterioles, lower through the capillaries, and falling slowly to near zero in the veins and at the right atrium.

velocity-area.d: Blood velocity equals flow divided by the total cross-sectional area of the vessels at that level. The capillaries together have the largest total area, so blood moves slowest there, about 0.3 mm/s, compared with about 30 cm/s in the aorta.

bp-measurement.d: Measuring arterial pressure with a sphygmomanometer: a cuff squeezes the brachial artery shut and is slowly let down. The first Korotkoff sound marks systolic pressure and the last marks diastolic pressure. A cuff that is too small or an arm below heart level gives a reading that is too high.

cardiac-output.d: The volume of blood one ventricle pumps per minute: heart rate times stroke volume (CO = HR × SV). It is about 5 L/min in a resting adult.

preload.d: The stretch on ventricular muscle at the end of filling, just before contraction, indexed by end-diastolic volume. It rises with greater venous return and with a longer filling time.

frank-starling.d: The heart's built-in property that a more-filled, more-stretched ventricle contracts more forcefully and ejects more, so stroke volume rises with end-diastolic volume. It keeps the outputs of the two ventricles matched.

contractility.d: The strength of contraction at any given stretch, set by how much calcium reaches the cross-bridges. Positive inotropic factors such as norepinephrine and epinephrine raise it; negative inotropic factors such as beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, acidosis and hyperkalemia lower it.

afterload.d: The pressure a ventricle must overcome to open its semilunar valve and eject blood, set mainly by aortic pressure for the left ventricle. A higher afterload leaves more blood in the ventricle after ejection and lowers stroke volume.

heart-rate-control.d: Heart rate is set by the cardiovascular center in the medulla oblongata. Its cardioaccelerator center speeds the SA node through sympathetic nerves and the cardiac plexus; its cardioinhibitory center slows it through the vagus nerves. Factors that change heart rate are called chronotropic.

cardiac-reserve.d: The difference between a person's highest cardiac output and their cardiac output at rest: the extra pumping available on demand. Training raises it; age and heart disease lower it.

capillary-diffusion.d: The net movement of each solute between plasma and interstitial fluid, down its own concentration gradient. Lipid-soluble substances such as oxygen and carbon dioxide pass through the endothelial cells; small water-soluble ones pass through the clefts between them.

capillary-hydrostatic.d: The pressure of blood against the inside of a capillary wall (CHP), also called blood hydrostatic pressure. It pushes fluid out of the capillary, and falls from about 35 mm Hg at the arteriole end to about 15 mm Hg at the venule end.

colloid-osmotic.d: The osmotic pressure made by dissolved proteins that cannot cross the wall between two fluids; also called oncotic pressure. In plasma (blood colloid osmotic pressure, BCOP) it is about 25 mm Hg, mostly from albumin, and it pulls fluid into capillaries.

net-filtration-capillary.d: The sum of the four Starling forces across a capillary wall: NFP = (CHP + IFCOP) − (BCOP + IFHP). A positive value means capillary filtration, fluid moving out; a negative value means capillary reabsorption, fluid moving in.

edema.d: An excess of fluid in the interstitial spaces, which forms when fluid filters out of capillaries faster than it drains away. Causes are higher capillary pressure, lower plasma protein, leaky capillary walls, or blocked drainage; widespread swelling is systemic edema.

map-co-tpr.t: mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output times resistance
map-co-tpr.d: The rule MAP = CO × TPR: mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. Because CO = heart rate × stroke volume, blood pressure can change only through heart rate, stroke volume or resistance.

baroreceptors.d: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the walls of the carotid sinuses and the aortic arch (the arch group is sometimes called the aortic sinuses, a name anatomists give to the bulges at the root of the aorta). They fire faster when arterial pressure stretches the wall more, and they reset to a new pressure within a day or two.

baroreceptor-reflex.d: The negative feedback loop that corrects fast changes in blood pressure: baroreceptor signals reach the cardiovascular center, which adjusts sympathetic and vagal output to the heart, arterioles and veins. Also called the baroreflex; on standing it is the orthostatic reflex.

orthostatic.d: A sustained fall in blood pressure on standing: at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes. Also called postural hypotension, it causes lightheadedness or fainting when the baroreceptor reflex cannot keep up.

autoregulation-local.d: A tissue's ability to adjust its own blood flow by changing the radius of its arterioles, without nerves or hormones. Metabolic autoregulation dilates arterioles when metabolites build up; the myogenic response constricts them when pressure stretches them.

atrial-reflex.d: A reflex in which stretch of the atria and nearby large veins, from more venous return, raises heart rate through the cardiovascular center. Also called the Bainbridge reflex.

exercise-cardiovascular.d: The changes exercise brings: higher heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output, arteriole dilation in working muscle, less flow to the gut and kidneys, and a modest rise in MAP. Target heart rate is a chosen percentage of maximum heart rate, which is roughly 220 minus age.

blood-volume-bp.t: blood volume and blood pressure (in detail)
blood-volume-bp.d: The link between how much blood you have and your long-term blood pressure: more volume raises venous return, stroke volume and cardiac output, so MAP rises; less volume lowers them. Only restoring volume corrects a lasting change.

kidney-volume-control.d: The principle that blood volume is set by how much sodium and water the kidneys excrete, the one loss route adjusted to match intake. Water follows sodium, so keeping sodium keeps fluid in the plasma and interstitial fluid.

raas-bp.d: The role of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system in raising blood pressure: low pressure makes the kidneys release renin, leading to angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles, releases aldosterone so the kidneys keep sodium and water, and triggers ADH and thirst.

adh-bp.d: The role of antidiuretic hormone in blood pressure: it makes the kidneys keep water, and at the high levels a large fall in volume produces, it also constricts arterioles. Its other name, vasopressin, reflects that effect.

anp-bp.d: The role of atrial natriuretic peptide in lowering blood pressure: released when the atria are stretched, it makes the kidneys excrete sodium and water, lowers renin, aldosterone and ADH, and relaxes arterioles.

hypertension.d: Arterial blood pressure that stays above normal on repeated measurements; by the American ACC/AHA guidelines (set in 2017 and kept in 2025), 130/80 mm Hg or more (stage 2 at 140/90 or more). Also called high blood pressure, it usually causes no symptoms but thickens the left ventricle and damages arteries over years.

atherosclerosis.d: The buildup of plaques of fat, foam cells and fibrous tissue in the tunica intima of large and medium arteries. Plaques narrow the lumen and can rupture, triggering a thrombus that blocks the artery.

heart-failure.d: A condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs, or can only do so at abnormally high filling pressures. Left-sided failure backs blood up into the lungs; right-sided failure backs it up into the systemic veins; congestive heart failure names the resulting congestion.

shock.d: Failure of the circulation to deliver enough oxygen to the tissues, so cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and lactate rises. Hypovolemic shock comes from too little volume, cardiogenic shock from a failing pump, and obstructive shock from a blockage of flow into or out of the heart.

distributive-shock.d: Shock caused by widespread vasodilation, which drops TPR and pools blood in dilated vessels; also called vascular shock. Its main forms are septic shock (from sepsis, the body's poorly controlled response to an infection), neurogenic shock (loss of sympathetic tone) and shock from a severe allergic reaction.

hemorrhage-compensation.d: The body's responses to blood loss: the baroreceptor reflex within seconds, movement of interstitial fluid into the plasma over hours, the RAAS, ADH and thirst over a day, and replacement of plasma proteins and red blood cells over days to weeks.

lymph.d: Interstitial fluid once it has entered a lymphatic vessel: mostly water and small solutes, with some protein, lymphocytes and anything picked up from the tissues.

lymphatic-vessels.d: The one-way vessels that return filtered fluid to the blood: blind-ended lymphatic capillaries, valved collecting vessels, lymphatic trunks, and the thoracic duct (from the cisterna chyli) and right lymphatic duct, which empty where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet.

lymph-node.d: A small, bean-shaped organ along the lymphatic vessels that filters lymph. Lymph enters through afferent vessels, trickles through macrophage-lined sinuses past a cortex of lymphoid nodules (with germinal centers) and a paracortex, and leaves through efferent vessels at the hilum; lymphocytes enter from the blood through high endothelial venules.

spleen.d: The largest lymphoid organ, in the upper left abdomen, which filters blood rather than lymph. Its white pulp holds lymphocytes around central arteries; its red pulp removes old red blood cells, platelets and bacteria and holds a platelet reserve.

lymphoid-organs.d: Primary lymphoid organs (red bone marrow and the thymus) are where lymphocytes are made and mature; secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, the spleen and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue such as the tonsils, Peyer's patches and BALT) are where mature lymphocytes meet antigens.

lymphedema.d: Protein-rich swelling of a region whose lymphatic drainage has failed, most often after lymph nodes are removed or irradiated, or from parasitic worms blocking the vessels. Over time the tissue becomes firm and non-pitting.

innate-vs-adaptive.d: Innate immunity is the defense present from birth that acts within minutes to hours against patterns shared by groups of microbes, the same way each time. Adaptive immunity is built by lymphocytes that each recognize one antigen; it takes days on first exposure and responds faster the next time.

barriers.d: The first line of defense: intact skin and mucous membranes, their secretions (mucus, tears, saliva, stomach acid) and resident harmless microbes, which keep most microbes from entering the tissues.

phagocytosis-immune.d: Killing of microbes by phagocytes, mainly neutrophils and macrophages: they find, bind, engulf and digest the microbe in a vesicle fused with lysosomes, using enzymes and an oxidative burst that makes superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and bleach.

nk-cell.d: A large granular lymphocyte of innate immunity that kills virus-infected and cancer cells without earlier exposure, when they show stress proteins or lack the normal self-identity protein; it releases granules that trigger the target's apoptosis.

inflammation.d: The local response to injury or infection: chemical messengers widen and open small vessels (redness, heat, swelling, pain), leukocytes leave the blood by rolling, sticking, diapedesis and chemotaxis toward chemokines, and phagocytes clear the site, leaving pus. Acute inflammation lasts days; chronic inflammation lasts weeks or more and scars.

fever.d: A rise in body temperature, usually to 38 °C or more, caused by pyrogens raising the hypothalamic set point through prostaglandin E2; heat-gain responses then raise temperature to meet the new set point.

complement.d: About 30 plasma proteins that, once activated by the classical, lectin or alternative pathway, split C3 and then coat microbes for phagocytes (opsonization), promote inflammation, and build the membrane attack complex that bursts microbes.

interferon.d: Cytokines released by virus-infected cells (interferon alpha and beta) that make neighboring cells produce antiviral proteins; interferon gamma, from NK cells and some lymphocytes, activates macrophages.

antimicrobial-proteins.d: Proteins made in advance that kill microbes directly: lysozyme, an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks bacterial cell walls, and defensins, small proteins that punch holes in microbial membranes.

pattern-recognition.d: Receptor proteins, such as the Toll-like receptors, that bind molecular patterns shared by groups of microbes (or released by damaged cells) and switch on cytokine release, starting the early induced immune response.

antigen.d: Any molecule that a lymphocyte's antigen receptor or an antibody binds specifically. Each antigen receptor binds one small part of it, an epitope (antigenic determinant), and a large antigen carries many epitopes.

t-cell.d: A lymphocyte that matures in the thymus (as a thymocyte, passing positive and negative selection) and recognizes, with its T cell receptor, only short peptides held on MHC proteins. Some kill infected cells; others coordinate responses.

b-cell.d: A lymphocyte that matures in the red bone marrow and binds intact antigen with a membrane-bound antibody as its antigen receptor; when activated, its descendants release antibodies.

mhc.d: Membrane glycoproteins coded by the major histocompatibility complex that hold peptides for T cells to inspect. Class I, on nearly all nucleated cells, shows peptides made inside the cell; class II, on antigen-presenting cells, shows peptides from material taken in. Their genes vary enormously between people (MHC polymorphism).

apc.d: A cell that takes in antigen, breaks it into peptides and loads them onto MHC class II (antigen processing), then displays them for T cells (antigen presentation): dendritic cells, which start naive T cell responses, macrophages and B cells.

self-tolerance.d: The state in which lymphocytes do not attack your own tissues. Central tolerance removes self-reactive lymphocytes as they mature (negative selection and clonal deletion in the thymus, a similar test in the marrow); peripheral tolerance silences those that escape, for example by clonal anergy when a T cell binds self antigen without a second, confirming signal.

clonal-selection.d: Activation of only the rare naive lymphocytes whose ready-made antigen receptors fit an antigen, followed by clonal expansion into a clone of identical cells; many clones responding to one microbe's many epitopes make a polyclonal response.

immune-memory.d: The ability to respond faster and more strongly to an antigen met before, carried by long-lived memory B cells and memory T cells left after clonal expansion, which are more numerous and quicker to switch on than the naive cells they came from.

helper-t.d: A CD4 T cell that recognizes antigen in MHC class II and, once activated, directs other immune cells with cytokines and surface contact. Th1 cells arm macrophages and cytotoxic T cells against microbes inside cells; Th2 cells direct the response to parasitic worms.

cytotoxic-t.d: A CD8 T cell that recognizes antigen in MHC class I and kills the cell showing it, by releasing perforin (which makes pores) and granzymes (which trigger caspases) or by binding Fas with its Fas ligand, so the target dies by apoptosis.

regulatory-t.d: A CD4 T cell, set up by the gene-control protein FOXP3, that suppresses other lymphocytes with IL-10 and TGF-beta, by taking up IL-2 and by removing B7 from dendritic cells. It keeps responses to self in check and ends responses after an infection.

t-activation.d: The switching on of a naïve T cell in a lymph node, which needs recognition of its peptide in MHC (signal 1), costimulation by B7 binding CD28 (signal 2) and cytokines (signal 3). IL-2 then drives clonal expansion into effector T cells and memory T cells.

transplant-rejection.d: Immune destruction of a transplanted organ or tissue, mostly by recipient T cells reacting to the donor's HLA (MHC) proteins: hyperacute (minutes, existing antibodies), acute (days to months, T cells) or chronic (months to years). Tissue typing matches HLA; in graft-versus-host disease, donor T cells attack the recipient.

plasma-cell.d: A fully differentiated B cell, packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum, that releases large amounts of one antibody. Activation needs helper T cell help for T cell-dependent (protein) antigens but not for T cell-independent antigens such as repeating capsule sugars.

antibody-structure.d: An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds. The variable regions at the arm tips form two antigen-binding sites; the constant regions, including the Fc region of the stem, set the class and bind Fc receptor proteins and complement.

antibody-classes.d: The five kinds of antibody, set by the heavy chain: IgG (main blood antibody, crosses to the fetus), IgA (in secretions), IgM (first made, a pentamer), IgE (on mast cells) and IgD (on naïve B cells). Class switching changes a B cell's class while keeping its variable region.

antibody-actions.d: The ways antibodies disable antigens: neutralization (blocking toxins and viruses from binding cells), agglutination (clumping), opsonization (coating for phagocytes), complement activation and directing natural killer cells. The antibody binds; other cells and proteins do the killing.

primary-secondary-response.d: The primary response to a first exposure has a lag of about 5–10 days and a low peak, mostly IgM then IgG. The secondary response to a later exposure comes from memory cells: faster, much higher, mostly IgG and better fitting. Seroconversion is when antibody first becomes detectable in the blood.

active-passive.d: Active immunity is made by your own immune system, after infection or a vaccine; it is slow to start, leaves memory and lasts long. Passive immunity is borrowed antibody, from mother to baby or by injection; it works at once but fades in weeks to months.
